query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dominant mechanism governing wear performance in high-entropy alloy protective coatings is the formation of a stable, fine-grained oxide (glaze) tribolayer at the surface. This layer, promoted by refined microstructures, enhances local hardness and reduces adhesive and plastic deformation wear during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy protective coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-based) processed to have a coarse-grained microstructure typical of standard processing.
generation.intervention: Modify the processing (e.g., via rapid solidification, severe plastic deformation, or heat-treatment) to produce a fine-grained version of the same coating, while keeping the composition constant.
generation.conditions: Perform reciprocating sliding wear tests in ambient air at varied loads and sliding speeds (covering both low and high regimes) to allow for frictional heating and oxide formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain size of the surface: fine grains increase the density of grain boundaries, which in turn promote the formation of a more continuous and adherent oxide tribolayer during wear.
generation.mechanism: A finer grain structure increases the intrinsic surface hardness and facilitates the generation of a uniform, stable oxide layer during friction. This tribolayer acts as a lubricating and protective barrier that reduces the initiation of cracks, mitigates plastic deformation and delamination, and thereby lowers both the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline coarse-grained coating, the fine-grained coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced specific wear rate, with scanning electron microscopy revealing a more intact and less cracked oxide layer on the wear track.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained high-entropy alloy coatings, which tend to form less uniform oxide layers that are prone to cracking and delamination, leading to higher friction and wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA coatings of similar chemistries (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or related systems) under ambient tribological conditions where oxidation is contributory. In inert atmospheres the absence of oxygen may limit oxide layer formation, thereby possibly altering the dominant wear mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical grain size below which the oxide layer becomes optimally stable and the quantitative relationship between grain refinement and wear rate require further definition. Compositional variations may also influence the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings with identical compositions: one with a coarse-grained microstructure (baseline) and the other processed to achieve a fine-grained microstructure. Perform standardized reciprocating sliding wear tests in ambient air over a range of loads and sliding speeds. Post-test evaluations will include friction coefficient measurement, wear rate determination, and detailed surface microstructural analysis using SEM/EDS to assess oxide layer integrity.
measurements: Morphology and continuity of the oxide tribolayer (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained coatings do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower friction coefficients, reduced wear rates, and a more continuous, adherent oxide layer) compared to the coarse-grained baseline, then the hypothesis that grain-refinement mediated oxide tribolayer stability governs wear performance is falsified.

Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.
